answer.rationale:
The strongest signal is temporal: a release shipped 2 hours ago and write-path p99 began climbing 90 minutes ago, which fits a release-induced regression better than an organic capacity problem. memory_b1 records a rollback clearing a similar spike, so I want the original record to check whether that case actually resembled this one (write-path latency vs. checkout errors, and whether causality was confirmed or just assumed from correlation). memory_b2 is the main competing direction because the degradation is region-confined, which superficially matches the March failover win; I want the source to see whether that event was write-heavy at peak, since failover during peak settlement writes is the one option that directly threatens the primary objective of not losing customer writes. That asymmetry is why I lean rollback: it is reversible and write-preserving, whereas failover puts in-flight writes at risk and add_capacity/replica routing (memory_b3, memory_b5) address read and queue pressure that is not what is being reported here. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) contained an external partner outage, not an internal write-path regression, so it treats a symptom.

I am holding this loosely. Each inherited memory is a compressed success story, and success stories systematically omit the cases where the same action was tried and did nothing. I do not know the base rate of failed rollbacks here, so the memory set is outcome-biased toward whatever was done and remembered. That is the specific downstream risk: if I commit broadly on a summary and it is a bad causal attribution, my action becomes the next memory and hardens the error for future sessions. I also cannot rule out that the release is coincidental and something region-local is degrading, or that the release included a non-reversible migration in which case a naive rollback is actively harmful. So I intend a small guarded rollback on a limited cohort first, consistent with memory_b6's finding that canary cohorts surface regressions inside an hour: if latency recovers in that cohort I have causal evidence and can widen; if it does not, I have cheaply eliminated the leading hypothesis and preserved the one intervention window's information value rather than spending it on a broad bet.
